items.tx: A while ago I was told a story; somebody's grandma, who lived in Donetsk, went to Volnovakha to pick up her Ukrainian pension in February 2022 (cash-only), and got caught up in the beginning of the SMO. She decided to go to Mariupol "until things calm down". A relative of hers was living at a dormitory adjacent to Azovstal, so she went there (terrible luck on that woman). The dorm was taken over by Azov fighters, who kept everyone who was still there as hostages. Absolute minimum of food and water, and no food at all after a week or so. At some point, they realized the Ukrainian soldiers would run into the basement anytime a Russian drone was close enough to be heard, and used that to flee. The old woman and her relative dashed through the kill zone and managed to avoid drones, bombs and snipers, and safely reached the Russian lines. It's a crazy story, the chain of bad luck and picking the worst possible new place to go at every spot, but after listening to the story what stuck with me was: oh yeah, she was kidnapped and taken hostage by Azov and used as a human shield. That's a thing that happened. And it registers to me as "normal" because that's just a thing they did and still do and despite constituting the worst series of war crimes Europe has seen since the Balkans, comparable only to ISIS in Syria, it's not even "shocking" to me anymore because of how much exposure to this terrible sort of thing I had and how nobody outside of Russia cares *at all*

items.t: The most beautiful woman in the word, and one of the unhappiest Princess Fawzia of Persia, photographed by Cecil Beaton in 1942. A year after this picture was…
items.tx:
The most beautiful woman in the word, and one of the unhappiest

Princess Fawzia of Persia, photographed by Cecil Beaton in 1942. A year after this picture was taken, Fawzia gave birth to a daughter, Princess Shahnaz Pahlavi, in Tehran. Given the Pahlavi dynasty’s need to secure the succession, the child’s sex was a disappointment. It was yet another blow for the lovely princess. Eighteen months earlier, Fawzia, the daughter of King Fuad I, and sister of King Farouk, had been forced to wed Crown Prince Mohammad Pahlavi in Cairo, in a wildly extravagant ceremony. A thousand doves were released, and caviar worth $1 million had been served to guests, including heads of state and European royals. But the union was purely dynastic and soon became hostile. Fawzia was seventeen; the crown prince, nineteen, and they had met only once. Moreover, her husband bitterly resented her fame. Fawzia’s astonishing pulchritude made her an international celebrity, and Cecil Beaton photographed her for Life magazine. Usually critical of his subjects, Beaton described her as an “Asian Venus” with a perfect heart-shaped face and pale blue-green eyes “the colour of the Indian Ocean at dawn”. She appeared in numerous magazines as the most beautiful and elegant woman in the world. But she was already taking pills. Raised in the cosmopolitan court of Cairo, Fawzia found Tehran intolerably restrictive. She never mastered Persian, which left her isolated and dependent on frequently treacherous translators. Relations with her mother-in-law, Queen Tadj ol-Molouk, were strained to say the least; the two argued frequently about Fawzia’s Western tastes, and her smoking and drinking in public, as well as her “unseemly” habit of driving a sports car, and her fascination with Hollywood films. Contemporaries described her as desperately lonely, finding excuses to return to Egypt for medical or family reasons. In 1945 Fawzia absconded from Persia and obtained a divorce. She paid for it bitterly. Under the settlement, her daughter Shahnaz remained in Iran - she was told her mother had left because “she didn’t love you”, and by the time she was a teenager had become clinically depressed. Fawzia withdrew from the public eye. In 1949 she married an Egyptian diplomat and the couple lived quietly in Alexandria, avoiding the press. She remained in Egypt after the 1952 revolution, spending her later years in complete seclusion, until her death in 2013 aged 91. The portrait below shows a young woman as the embodiment of royal perfection. But behind the glamour was a loveless marriage, a court that despised her, and a daughter she lost.
